The rule this list applies

Cold outreach from this year, where more than 40 days have passed since either side last spoke, matched to a relevant blog. Breweries first.

Nobody on the Follow-Up List qualifies, because that cascade only started on 17 August, so the oldest contact on it is a fortnight old. The 40 day rule reaches back into the earlier 2026 batches instead, most of which never made it onto this board. The candidates came from sweeping Sent Items across the whole of 2026, which took three windows because the Outlook connector stops paging at 1,000 messages and the year holds more than that.

Every thread below was read in full, both directions, before it was listed. That is what separates the two groups on this page.

Fix 1 — the follow-up now chases what was actually agreed. Aidan caught the Lead Forensics cascade generating the wrong chase on Fullwoodhead Dairy Supplies. Neil Wilson had agreed on the phone to forward the email to his colleagues, so the only live question was whether they came back to him — but the generated follow-up re-ran the website-visit pitch (the reason the first email existed, which Neil had already read) and then closed by asking "are you the best person to speak to about this", a question he had answered on the call. The cause was structural, not a wording slip: buildLeadForensicsBumpEmail composed from the stage plus initialType ('call' or 'email') and nothing else, so "he'll forward it to colleagues", "he asked me to send a datasheet" and "he said try Dave instead" all produced identical text — every call-led lead would get the same wrong chase, and it did: Dave Goodwin at Wily Fox was asked who the right person was on the follow-up when the initial had already asked him exactly that. There is now a followUp.initialCommitment field, auto-populated by the morning check from Aidan's own initial email in Sent Items rather than typed in — the commitment is almost always written down in his opening line ("thanks for your time on the phone just now and for agreeing to forward this onto your colleagues"). The patterns it looks for are documented in the code above the function. Fullwoodhead's fu1 now reads "I hope you're well, I just wanted to follow up on our discussion yesterday to see if you've had any feedback from your colleagues on the email I sent? Thanks again!" and fu2 chases the same thing more lightly. Where nothing was agreed — a cold email off a website visit, or a voicemail with no commitment, as on Sagetech and Mantec — the field is deliberately left absent and the copy falls back to a short honest chase that still doesn't re-pitch. Two of the nine Lead Forensics leads had a genuine stated commitment to parse; the other seven honestly did not. Separately, the "are you the best person" closer is now only asked while that question is genuinely open: never after a call, never once the contact has answered it (rightPersonConfirmed), and never when a commitment is being chased. The fault was one level down: the predicate deciding which contacts to offer, isActionableContact, counted active as actionable. That is a fair definition of "not retired", but the wrong one for this page, whose whole purpose is people who have not been written to yet. Because Jason sat first in the contacts array he became the tile's primary contact — his name headlined the card, "Open all 3 in Outlook" would have drafted him a second cold pitch hours after the real one, and the two people who actually needed emailing were buried under "+2 more contacts". Fixed by separating the two ideas: isColdContact (strictly not-started) now drives the tile's primary contact, its contact count, the drafts listed inside it and the "Open all in Outlook" button, so a contact mid-cascade can never be re-drafted from here; and inCascadeContacts surfaces the colleagues who are already being chased as a note on the tile — "Already in the follow-up cascade at QV Foods: Jason Munden (initial earlier today)" — rather than silently dropping them, so the card still tells the whole truth about the account. Verified in the sandbox across all three leads currently on the desk: QV Foods now leads with Jonathan Pedley, Kingsland Drinks with John Allen (and notes Phil Rutter, who is sitting in needs-review), Higgidy with Matt Mantell, and "Open all" drafts only ever reach the genuinely cold addresses. Only QV Foods was actually affected — it was the one lead with a live active contact alongside new cold ones — but the same fault would have hit every future leaver-replacement lead where a colleague was still in the cascade, which is now the common case. 26 Aug update, fourth refresh — a click on this page now survives the next refresh. Aidan: "for the last two portals I marked Morris Lubricants as remove from cascade, then when I ask you to refresh the portal it's back in the replied / needs your call list." He was right, twice, and it was not his fault. This file has no backend: pressing a button only ever changed that browser tab's copy of the data, and the only route back was noticing a small green "Copy Sync Prompt" button in the header and pasting its clipboard text into the chat. Miss that and the next portal — rebuilt from the copy on Claude's side, which never heard about the click — silently discarded it. Quietly losing somebody's work is the worst behaviour available here, so there are now three lines of defence. First, the page saves itself. Opened as the published artifact, the portal can publish a new version of its own document: on any change it re-reads its own source, splices the current data back between two markers around the lead arrays, and publishes that — so the click becomes part of the page, and the next refresh reads it with nothing to paste. It rebuilds from its own fetched source rather than from the rendered DOM, so the file does not grow or drift with each save, and repeated saves stay clean (verified by round-tripping a real removal through a publish and booting the result: 135 Tapflo and 38 Sychem leads, 181 and 44 contacts, both arrays byte-identical, the removal intact, and the page still rendering). Rapid clicks are batched into one save, and nothing is ever published on page load. Second, if that is not available — the file was opened as a plain download rather than the artifact, or the viewer only has read-only access — a bar pins itself to the top of the page and says so in as many words, lists exactly what is unsaved, and offers the clipboard hand-off. It never claims to have saved something it hasn't; a publish conflict or a read-only view is reported as a failure with what to do next. Third, the tab will not close quietly while anything is still unsaved. The "Remove from cascade" confirmation now also points at the bar, so the honest state of play is visible at the moment of the click rather than discovered a day later. Deliberately still not using localStorage: this file is opened from too many different places for browser storage to be dependable, and appearing to save and then not is the exact failure being fixed. Aidan's Sent Items lesson applied to this batch too: deduping against Sent Items rather than only Salesforce and this board caught four more collisions in these 35 — Joshua Smedley and George Howell at Belhaven were already in Jay's 12–13 Aug "Flow Meters" thread and are now active off those real sends; Alan Hutchison at North British was emailed by Jay twice (27 Jul, 4 Aug) and was missing from the board entirely, so he has been added as active; Craig Murphy at Loch Lomond was introduced by Jay on 10 Jul and is now active; and Simon Steele at Alcohols, emailed by Aidan on 2 Jun 2025 with Stephen Eastcott cc'd, stays startable but carries a prior-contact warning so nobody introduces Tapflo to him from scratch. Jay's Sent Items could not be read in full: the connector caps paging at offset 1000 and his folder holds 3,275 messages, so roughly 3 Jun–30 Jul of his outbound was never scanned — a lead whose only prior contact was from Jay in that window can still look new. And the desk now stands at 54 rather than the 35 target, because both runs each sourced a full batch; that is over-supply rather than a miss, and the honest read is that some of those 54 are companies where a colleague has already emailed someone. Latent bug worth a look, found by the pre-ship render check and not introduced today: nine leads carry no pitch object (Isle of Wight Distillery, iFlow, We Love Coffee, Sagetech Medical, Wily Fox, Mantec, Fullwoodhead, 2 Sisters via Rubix, DQD Engineering). Their in-cascade contacts are all flagged lead_forensics so the follow-up builder avoids it today, but buildMailshotEmail reads lead.pitch.subject before that check, so the first of them to reach the mailshot stage would throw and take the whole Follow-Up List render down with it. 1 Sep, second round, all four points raised by Aidan, plus a collision to explain. The 08:30 scheduled run and this session both published to this artifact within an hour of each other. The scheduled run read the board at 08:30, worked for two hours, and published at 10:51 on top of a baseline that predated this morning’s corrections, so it never saw the Sent Items dedupe. Nothing it published has been deleted. Where both versions held the same company, the verified version replaced it; where only the scheduled run had it, the lead stays with a warning. 14 of its 48 new leads are provably already worked and have been retired rather than emailed: Stourgarden, Nichols/Vimto, Volac, Aimia Foods, New England Seafood, Glenmorangie, Brothers Cider, Industrial Chemicals, James Briggs, Exol Lubricants, Westland Horticulture and Greenhalghs all hard-bounced or were spam-rejected on 27 and 28 Aug; Polyseam bounced on Jay’s 27 Aug send; Teal & Mackrill had a two-way exchange with Aidan in Nov 2025. The remaining 34 carry an UNVERIFIED banner on the card until someone checks them against Sent Items. Desk back to 35 verified. Six leads added this round (Bartoline, Vickers Oils, Metalube, Meridian Foods, Renshaw, GB Lubricants) from 33 screened, and the Sent Items check killed five more that Salesforce had cleared, including Esschem Europe (Jay, July) and ReAgent (Aidan, replied twice). Renshaw carries a warning: both contacts sit on legacy domains that may bounce. Pieminister has the right contact. Anna Setterfield’s 27 Aug out-of-office routed production enquiries to Mike Werrett, Production Manager, and the earlier run missed it because the search preview cut off above the routing block. His address is recorded exactly as she typed it, Mike.werret@ with one t against a surname spelled with two, so watch for a bounce. The same reply named a Technical Manager and a QA Manager; neither was added, because at a food manufacturer those titles own hygiene and quality rather than the pumps. The Outlook button now works in the Interested and Needs-your-call sections. Both only ever linked the customer’s reply, or failing that the very first send, and never looked at lastMessageId, so the last thing Aidan sent was unreachable from there. Raymond Lilley at iFlow surfaced it: his record had the right message ID on file all along and the page simply was not using it. Language rules are in force. Em dashes and en dashes are gone from the Tapflo lead data and from every piece of copy that reaches a customer: the bump-email openers, the Lead Forensics chasers, the mailshot intro and the case-study templates. 2,736 generated emails were rendered and checked to confirm it. Ranges read as 100 - 250. This follows the unslop v2.0 filter Tom supplied, which rates the em dash the highest-value fix on the list because Claude over-uses it where other models no longer do. Sychem is deliberately untouched and still contains its original dashes: the standing rule that nothing here changes Sychem automatically outranks the new language rule, so that stays Aidan’s call. Mobiles are no longer pulled. ZoomInfo is asked for business email, direct dial and switchboard only. Mobiles already on the board were left alone rather than deleted. 1 Sep, third change, raised by Aidan: three delivery failures were sitting in the wrong queue. Graham’s Family Dairy, Camerons Brewery and Halo Foods each had a card in Replied, needs your call that read “not delivered, but this is NOT a bad address”. That queue is for human replies waiting on a decision, and a bounced message is not a reply, so all three sat there looking like work that needed answering. They have moved into the retired bucket, which is now Opted out / bounced / removed / undeliverable, and that section has been taught the difference between a message that failed and an address that is dead. Everything in it now carries a failure type: 7 dead addresses where the recipient genuinely does not exist, 9 contacts who have left, and 7 that are still reachable, where the receiving server refused the message on spam or policy grounds or simply never answered. That last group is flagged amber, sorted to the top, and carries the address and the phone numbers on the card, because the mailbox is almost certainly live and a call or a resend from another address will land. Camerons is the clearest example: Barry Cuthbert’s message was rejected as spam by their domain, but Billy Watson at the same site received his fine, so the route in is open. Halo Foods is the one to watch, because Iain Brunnock is the only contact on that lead, so if it is not recovered the company drops off the board entirely. A count of each type now sits under the section heading. Merge repair, same hour, both parts flagged by Aidan. The first pass of this merge matched on company and then replaced the whole lead object, which is exactly the failure the refresh protocol warns about. It cost two things. Ten people the 08:30 run had added were dropped (Tony Brown at Swizzels, three at Energas, Alan Hutchison at North British, Trevor Parker at Norbev, Tony Brewerton at Loch Lomond, Callum Anderson at Crisp Malt, Stephen Evans at Pritchitts, Sean Pearce at Alcohols); all ten are back. And nine contacts had a settled decision quietly undone by being replaced with an earlier version of themselves. Those are restored too, most importantly Typhoo Tea, which Aidan removed himself on 27 Aug because it is a dry tea blending and packing site where the duty is vacuum and TSG sells fluid pumps; both contacts are excluded again and the company is off the desk. Angus Fire is likewise back to a company-level no: Chris Wylam replied that they have no chemical manufacturing in the UK, so he is negative, Graham Crook and Paul Upton are excluded, and Jennifer Leith sits in needs-your-call on an unattributable bounce. Leo Group’s Barry Baxter returns to bounced, with a note recording that the attribution came from the Graph search index rather than a readable diagnostic, so it is reversible if Aidan knows better. The merge rule is now written up properly in the refresh protocol: union at contact level, and for a shared contact keep the more resolved status, never the one you happened to start from. 1 Sep, fourth change, and the principle behind it: this is Aidan’s cascade, not the team’s. Four contacts were sitting in his follow-up queue on threads Jay Lamb had opened from his own mailbox: Alan Hutchison at North British Distillery, Craig Murphy at Loch Lomond Group, and Joshua Smedley and George Howell at Belhaven Brewery. The portal was about to tell Aidan to send a 3 Day Follow Up on somebody else’s email. All four are out of the cascade, marked ownedBy: Jay, and kept on the board only so nobody re-sources them as fresh cold leads. Polyseam is labelled the same way. The rule from here: the delegate mailboxes are read for two things only. One, deduplication, so Aidan never cold-emails a company a colleague is already working, which is the check that saved five leads earlier today. Two, the email and call volume on the Team Performance page, which is the one place Jay’s and Beth’s activity belongs. A send from their mailbox must never create a follow-up, advance a cascade stage, or put a card in Aidan’s queue. Where a colleague is already in a live thread, the company stays visible with a NOT YOURS TO CHASE banner naming who owns it, rather than being deleted, because deleting it is how it gets re-sourced next month. 1 Sep, fifth change, both points raised by Aidan. Leo Group is off the list. Leo Savry replied on 28 Aug with “I will pass on the relevant guys” and copied in Michael Meays, and Aidan has confirmed the emails were forwarded on internally, so all six contacts there are out of the cascade and the company is off the Cold Lead Action Desk. Nothing is deleted: the lead stays on the board with the reason written onto it, because deleting it is how it comes back as a fresh cold lead next month, and the bounce evidence on Barry Baxter and the leaver response on Vasile Vlad are both preserved in their history. If Michael Meays or one of the relevant guys comes back, that is an inbound and the lead can be reinstated with Undo. Desk goes from 58 to 57. We Love Coffee was asking Aidan to answer an email he had already answered. Hollie Gallacher’s 25 Aug reply, “It was Laura! I’ve forwarded this across”, was sitting in Replied, needs your call. He had in fact replied at 07:49 on 27 Aug: “Thank for your help Hollie, its much appreciated!” The earlier run logged her inbound reply but never checked Sent Items for his outbound answer on the same thread, which is why the card stayed open. Her card is now retired and the 27 Aug reply is linked from it. The useful part of that lead is what is left behind: Laura is the real prospect, she was sent the enquiry on 25 Aug, she has not been in touch in the week since, and there is still no surname or email address for her, so the switchboard is the only route in. The general rule this exposes: a card only belongs in Replied, needs your call if the last message on the thread came from them. If Aidan has sent the most recent message, the ball is on their side and the card belongs in the cascade or in the retired bucket, never in the queue asking him for a decision he has already made. 1 Sep, sixth change, raised by Aidan on AK Stoddart: weak fallbacks are not included any more. A weak fallback is a contact the sourcing added only to fill a slot, flagged in its own notes, usually a food-safety or QA “Technical Manager” at a food or drink manufacturer, where that title owns hygiene and quality rather than the pumps. Seven never-emailed weak fallbacks were removed: Holly McHarg and Gordon Campbell at AK Stoddart, Andrew Pentland at Willowbrook Foods, Abdul Bahar at Greenhalghs Craft Bakery, Kevin Elvidge at Bartoline, Peter Crinyion at Renshaw, and Vishaka Naique, who was the only contact on Delice de France, so that whole lead came off the board. Every company except Delice de France keeps a real contact: AK Stoddart still has Grant McMichael, the one genuine engineering title, plus the three general managers Aidan already emailed on 27 Aug. Only never-contacted fallbacks were touched. A weak fallback that had already been emailed is a live thread, not a fallback, and stays exactly where it is. The rule from here: the sourcing does not add weak fallbacks at all. If a company’s only route in is a QA or admin title with no engineering or operations owner, the honest answer is one strong contact or none, not a padded list. 1 Sep, seventh change, spotted by Aidan on GeoPura: the “Reply to this email” button was opening the wrong email. On Omar Ramadan’s card it pulled up Aidan’s own first outreach from 25 Aug instead of Omar’s 26 Aug reply. The cause was a fallback in the card code: when a reply had no Outlook ID stored against it, the button quietly used the initial send’s ID instead, so it always opened something and never admitted it was the wrong thing. Ten cards on this board carry a quoted reply and five of them had no reply ID at all, so the button was lying on half of them: GeoPura, Kingsland Drinks, Wily Fox Brewery, Lionel Hitchen and DQD Engineering. All five IDs have been recovered from Outlook and written on, so every reply card now links to the real message. The fallback is gone: a button that says “Reply to this email” now points at their email or does not appear, and where an ID genuinely cannot be found the card says so in amber and tells you to reply from inside your own last sent email instead. Better a missing button than a button that opens the wrong thing. One thing turned up while checking: Helen McNair at Lionel Hitchen was filed as bounced with no failure type, but nothing ever bounced. She wrote to say she was leaving and to speak to the maintenance manager or project engineering manager instead. She is now correctly marked as a contact who has left, with the address flagged as still valid, which her own later email proves: she wrote again on 27 Aug about a Hygiena partnership, a different subject and not a pump enquiry. She named two roles but no names or addresses, so no replacement contact was added. 1 Sep, eighth change: four decisions synced out of the browser tab. These were made by clicking buttons on the page and had never reached the file, which is exactly the failure this board was rebuilt to stop. Phil Rutter at Kingsland Drinks is out of the cascade. He was a referral rather than a rejection, and John Allen and Mark Bonner are both live on the same lead from that referral, so the company is still being worked. Simon Ballard at PIL Membranes moves to interested and chasing, with a chase-by date of 8 Sep: Aidan has offered him a cost review on the three Robuschi units he just bought and wants a meeting out of it. Jennifer Leith at Angus Fire is out, and that closes the company: she never replied, and Chris Wylam answered instead to say Angus have no chemical manufacturing in the UK. With Paul Upton and Graham Crook already excluded and Chris marked negative, no live contact remains, and the lead stays on the board only so it is not re-sourced. Richard Ramsay at WD-40 is marked negative. His reply came through the sync as a placeholder, so his real words were written onto the record: “Can I please ask how you got my contact details? Please be aware that we do not use any pump systems in WD-40 Company.” That is a company-level no, so it took two colleagues with it. Karen Appleton and Philip Tweed were both still active at WD-40 and have been retired under the same rule already applied to Angus Fire: a site that says it uses no pumps at all will give the same answer to the next person we email there. Both are reversible if that reading is wrong. One wording change: the synced note for Richard arrived with an em dash in it, which the language rules on this board forbid, so it reads “Replied negatively, opted out” instead. 1 Sep, ninth change: the same sync came through twice, and the second copy carried two extra lines. Four of the six events had already been written to the file in the previous sync, with identical wording: Phil Rutter, Simon Ballard, Jennifer Leith and Richard Ramsay. Those were skipped rather than replayed, because pushing them again would have stamped every one of those cards with a duplicate history entry and made the record read as though each decision had been taken twice. A board-wide check now confirms zero contacts carry a repeated history line. Darin Smith at Burts Potato Chips moves to interested and chasing, chase by 8 Sep: Aidan replied on 1 Sep and wants to be prompted if Darin goes quiet. Michael Kendall at Wholebake goes back to active but pausedUntilStage: "checkin", which parks his next touch at the 30 day check-in instead of running him through the fast 3 day and 7 day chase. Two facts were written onto his record while it sits parked: Wholebake’s only other contact, David Crain, hard-bounced, so Michael is the single live route into that company, and the auto-reply on his thread came from James Clark saying he had left and to contact Charlie Morgan, with no address supplied, so Charlie is deliberately not on the board as a guessed contact. Needs your call is now empty for the first time since this board was built. 1 Sep, tenth change: the Outlook buttons were building the wrong kind of URL, and this time it was measured rather than guessed. Aidan hit “This message might have been moved or deleted” again on Open Last Sent Email. The previous three attempts at this all assumed the message ID was being mangled and kept adjusting the character conversion. The conversion was fine. 29 messages were pulled fresh from the mailbox and for every one of them the ID, converted and percent-encoded, matched Microsoft’s own webLink parameter exactly, including the hard case where the ID reads AAIW5f-mAAA= and Microsoft’s link reads AAIW5f%2FmAAA%3D. What was wrong was the address the ID was being pasted into. The page was building outlook.cloud.microsoft/mail/deeplink/read/<id>, a shape that was invented rather than taken from anywhere, and Outlook answers it with the moved-or-deleted screen even for a message sitting in the mailbox. Microsoft returns a guaranteed-good link for every message it hands over, and the page now builds that exact format instead. The generated URL was compared character by character against Microsoft’s own and is identical. All 592 message IDs stored on this board were checked at the same time: none are malformed, and the 29 held in one encoding and the 53 held in the other both come out correct through the same function. One live send was picked up while checking: Simon Ballard at PIL Membranes was chased again at 15:05 today, after the browser sync was captured, so that send is now on his record and his Outlook button points at it. The 8 Sep chase date is unchanged. 1 Sep, eleventh change: the fix was already in the file, and the tab was the problem. The screenshot of the failure shows the URL outlook.cloud.microsoft/mail/deeplink/read/..., which is the OLD address format. The version published before it builds outlook.office365.com/owa/?ItemID=... instead, and only one function on the whole page builds that link, so the page in that tab was the previous build. Checked properly rather than assumed: Sean Carroll’s stored ID was fetched live from the mailbox, the message is present and readable, and the link the current code generates for it is character for character identical to Microsoft’s own webLink for that same message. Nothing was wrong with his record. A build stamp now sits under the tab switcher in the header reading, for example, build 2026-09-01e. This page republishes itself whenever a button is clicked, so an open tab can hold week-old code while the saved file is current, and from the outside a fixed file and a stale tab look exactly the same. That ambiguity cost most of three rounds on this bug. If the stamp does not match what was last shipped, the page needs a reload, and now that can be checked in a second instead of debugged. 1 Sep, twelfth change: still failing, so this stops guessing and starts gathering evidence. Two URL formats have now been tried and both fail in Aidan’s browser: the original outlook.cloud.microsoft/mail/deeplink/read/ and Microsoft’s own outlook.office365.com/owa/?ItemID= webLink format, the second of which was proved byte-identical to what Microsoft returns for the exact message on the card. The data is not the problem: Sean Carroll’s stored ID was fetched live and the message is present and readable. This sandbox cannot open a browser against Outlook, so a third guess would be worth no more than the first two. Three things changed instead. An alternate link is now offered on the card, on the standard OWA host outlook.office.com/mail/deeplink/read/, which is not the host the original broken version used. A copy-the-link button sits next to it, because the URL from a failed attempt is the one piece of evidence that cannot be gathered from this side. An ampersand-escaping bug was found and fixed while doing this: the webLink format is the first of these URLs to contain a query string, and it was being written into an onclick attribute with bare & characters. Browsers usually tolerate that, so it is unlikely to be the whole story, but it was wrong and it is now escaped properly in all three places a card can offer an Outlook button. Whichever link works settles it, and the other one gets deleted. 1 Sep, thirteenth change, and the approach changes rather than the guess. Three item-ID deep links have now failed in Aidan’s browser: outlook.cloud.microsoft/mail/deeplink/read, outlook.office365.com/owa/?ItemID= (Microsoft’s own webLink format, proved byte-identical to what Graph returns for the exact message) and outlook.office.com/mail/deeplink/read. Every time, the message was confirmed present and readable in the mailbox. A fourth guess at a URL was not worth making from an environment that cannot open a browser against Outlook. What settled it was Aidan’s own screenshot of the Jardox email: he found it by typing the subject into Outlook’s search box and got exactly one result. So the finding was never the hard part, the item ID was. Every card with an Outlook button now carries a Find this email in Outlook search button that opens Outlook with the subject already typed in, with any Re: or Fwd: prefix stripped. A search URL carries no message ID, so there is nothing to encode wrongly, nothing that breaks when a message moves folders, and nothing that depends on which ID format the host will accept. It also fails softly: the worst case is an empty search box rather than an error page. The host used is outlook.cloud.microsoft, because that is where Aidan’s own session demonstrably lives according to the address bar in the failures. The two ID-based links are still on the card, demoted to “try the direct link” and “copy the direct link”, so if one of them does start working the evidence is still there to promote it back. 1 Sep, build h, and an answer to the fair question of what happened, because the honest answer is nothing did. Every saved copy of this file, from the earliest one this morning through to the version in use an hour ago, builds the Outlook link with the identical line of code. It was never repaired and then broken again. It was declared fixed three times on the strength of the wrong check: each round verified that the page produced the URL that had been intended, which is not the same thing as the button opening the email, and only the second of those can be tested from a machine with no browser onto Outlook. The character encoding really was verified properly against 29 live messages, and that part is genuinely correct, but a correct ID in an address Outlook will not accept still gets you nowhere. Two changes now make the next attempt cheap instead of expensive. The links are real anchors rather than window.open calls. An anchor can be right-clicked and copied, shows where it goes on hover, and cannot be silently swallowed by a popup blocker or by a sandbox that withholds popup permission. window.open with a window-size string is the most fragile way to leave a page and it gives no signal at all when it fails, so it could have been failing for a completely different reason to the one being chased. And the exact URLs are now printed on the card, behind a "show the exact links" toggle, as selectable text. Every round of this stalled on nobody knowing what the address bar actually said. One screenshot of the card now answers that. 2 Sep update, morning check. Both copies of this board were byte identical when read, so nothing was lost or reverted in the merge. Cascade tracking is fully in sync: a 739 message sweep of Aidan’s Sent Items back to 4 June found no send that this board was missing, and no not-started contact has been emailed inside the current campaign. The morning’s real finding came from the dedupe that the 1 Sep 08:30 run never got to. Thirty-four leads were still carrying an UNVERIFIED flag; all thirty-four have now been checked, against Jay Lamb’s and Beth Blunden’s mailboxes on name and domain, and against Aidan’s own mailbox across every folder and every date. Three more companies turned out to be a colleague’s, not Aidan’s: The Authentic Food Company (Jay emailed Scott Smart plus two others on 17 Jul), Harvey & Son of Lewes (Jay emailed Miles Jenner at the exact address on this lead, 8 Jul) and Belhaven Brewery, now fully retired rather than half. All three carry the NOT YOURS TO CHASE banner with every contact excluded and ownedBy set. The same treatment has been finished off on North British Distillery, Loch Lomond Group and Belhaven, where the banner was already up but four, three and two contacts respectively were still sitting in Aidan’s queue as live cold cards, which is exactly what the rule is meant to prevent. Thirteen contacts across the six companies came off the desk. There is also an unsent draft in Aidan’s Drafts folder, dated 1 Sep, replying onto Jay’s North British thread to Alan Hutchison. It has not gone out. It is flagged on that lead and worth deleting. Prior contact of Aidan’s own turned up on three more leads that had looked untouched: Rich Chadderton at Purity Soft Drinks was emailed 13 and 14 Aug 2025, Aaron Gooch at Broadland Drinks on 11 Nov 2025, and Glanbia UK ran as a five-person campaign in Jan 2026. All are eight to twelve months cold so they stay startable, but each now says so in the why so nobody introduces Tapflo from scratch to somebody who already knows us. That same check retired Ashley Chadwick at Broadland Drinks, whose address failed with “550 invalid mailbox” back in Nov 2025 and had been sitting on the board ever since as a startable cold contact. Two leavers were being chased for a fortnight. Graham Horner’s 19 Aug auto-reply said he had left Agrivert, and Peter Martindale’s said he had retired from Kendal Nutricare and that the mailbox is unmonitored. Two earlier runs logged both as ordinary out-of-office notes, so a Next Day and a 3 Day Follow Up went into each. Both are now retired with deliveryIssue.kind set to contact_left. Darryl Hall, named in Peter’s own reply, has been added to Kendal Nutricare as his replacement. Agrivert now has no live route in at all, since Graham was its only contact, and that is flagged at the top of the lead. Three contacts named in routing blocks have been added after reading the full bodies rather than the previews: Steven Harper, Production Supervisor at Nairn’s, named by Gordon Clarkson who is away for an extended period; Ken Keetley, GM Specialist Coatings at Fujichem Sonneborn, named by Chris Hilton who is out to 8 Sep; and Simon Kemp, Maintenance Manager at Pukka Pies, whose email address ZoomInfo has now supplied, which was the only reason he was left off before. Five people named on the same route were deliberately not added and each says why on the lead: Pieter Jacobs at Nairn’s and Liam Severn at The Ice Co have no title and no ZoomInfo record, Kimberley Gooding at Gressingham has no title at a food manufacturer, Paul White at AK Stoddart has neither address nor title, and Heather Ditchfield at Rock Oil is a Technical Sales Consultant rather than a pump owner. Plater Group has converted. Salesforce Opportunity “Plater Chemicals - 20m³/h MagDrive” was raised on 1 Sep at £7,940.38, stage Quoted, owned by Stephen Eastcott, and Richard Sykes matches it on both Account name and email address. He is marked converted and his three colleagues are excluded, because cold-chasing a company that is already mid-quote is the wrong call. Arkell’s Brewery joins the board at its real state from the untracked-outreach sweep: Aidan emailed it on 18 Aug for Craig Brewin’s attention and it had never been recorded anywhere, so it goes on as active with the real send date and message ID rather than as a fresh cold lead. One contact only, because a 14 record ZoomInfo sweep found Craig Brewin is the single engineering title on site and the rest is commercial and pub-estate. Two other leftover domains were checked and left off honestly: Pyroplast Energy was a CC on the Clean Planet Energy thread rather than outreach of its own, and Treleavens was a Sychem ATP pitch, which is out of scope here. No new replies, no new bounces and no new out-of-office replies have arrived since the 1 Sep run: the newest inbound on any outreach thread is 31 Aug. Fifty-four leads are still startable against a target of 35, so no new sourcing was needed this morning. 2 Sep, second pass. Two changes to the cascade at Aidan’s request, then a new tab. The 3 Day Follow Up is gone. It was never a 3 day touch: across all 22 times it was ever sent the real gap from the initial email was 6 days three times, 7 days four times and 8 days fifteen times, and the stage table already carried it at gapDays 7, so the label was the only thing claiming three days. The cascade is now initial, next day, 7 day, 30 day check-in, then mailshots. Its long copy, the one Aidan rewrote on 24 Aug, moved onto the 7 Day rather than being deleted, and the 22 contacts who had already had the old 3 Day skip to the 30 day check-in because in practice they have already had a 7 day chase. The Next Day email no longer claims to be about yesterday. “my email from yesterday” was hardcoded and it was wrong most of the time: 21 of the 129 Next Day follow-ups already sent went out 3, 5 or 8 days after the initial while still saying yesterday, and every one of the 71 contacts queued for that stage was 6 to 15 days out, Arkell’s at 15. It now dates itself off the real send date through the same naturalDaysAgoPhrase() helper the Lead Forensics builder was already using, so it reads yesterday, then a day name, then last week, then a couple weeks ago. New tab, Suggested Mailshots. Cold outreach from this year that has gone quiet for more than 40 days, matched to relevant content. Nothing on the Follow-Up List qualifies, since that cascade only began on 17 Aug, so the candidates came from sweeping Sent Items across the whole of 2026, which needed three windows because the Outlook connector stops paging at 1,000 messages and the year holds 2,436. Breweries first, as asked. Of six brewery threads only three are safe to mail: Langham, Wold Top and Sulwath. Salopian said “we will in touch if appropriate”, Alfred’s said they have no requirements, and Burnt Mill is mid-deal with Joe on a 36 month ATP agreement, so all three are held back on screen with the quote that disqualified them. The Newt in Somerset is listed unverified because it is cider rather than beer and its reply has not been read. Content comes from a library of 227 URLs captured the same day, 50 case studies, 45 blog posts and 132 downloads, held in full in the project spec at claude/content-library.md. Worth knowing for future refreshes: the blog sitemap is stale and omits four live late-August peristaltic posts, and the blog index served a stale render on first request, so neither can be trusted alone.

Only outbound identified as customer/prospect-facing outreach and the inbound replies to it are counted below — internal TSG traffic, Salesforce/system notifications, HR/absence tools (Timetastic, Deskbird) and vendor marketing mail are excluded. Response rate is estimated: each rep's most recent 25 sent and 25 received items were read and classified by recipient/sender domain, then that ratio was scaled to the full 30-day total — the same sampling approach used elsewhere in TSG's internal reporting.

🔔 Replied — needs your call

A reply came in that the morning Outlook check couldn't confidently classify as clearly negative — have a quick read and mark it yourself. Tapflo only for now; see the footnote below.

🔄 Interested — chasing next step

Genuine interest, but it isn't a done deal and it isn't a real Salesforce enquiry yet — there's still legwork on your side (an EPCm to loop in, a call to actually get booked, someone to nudge) before it either lands as a real conversion or needs writing off. Not part of the cold cascade — these get chased manually, on your own timeline.

📬 Ready to send

Nothing being chased right now. Head to the Cold Lead Action Desk, open a draft in Outlook and send it, then click "Start Follow-Up Tracking" underneath that contact — it'll show up here the moment you do.

📅 Pending — coming up

Not due yet — just a preview so you can see what's next. Nothing here needs action; it moves up to "Ready to send" on its own due date (dates never land on a weekend or UK bank holiday — they roll to the next working day).

📭 Opted out / bounced / removed / undeliverable

Everyone out of the cascade, kept here as a record with the reason: opted out, replied negatively, removed by hand, or the email never landed. Removals are deliberately not counted as conversions. Not all of these are dead ends. A delivery failure where the receiving server rejected the message on spam or policy grounds means the address itself is almost certainly fine, so those are sorted to the top with an amber flag and are worth a phone call or a resend. A genuine unknown-recipient bounce is a dead address and sits below it in grey. The counts underneath say how many of each you have.
Tapflo leads: a scheduled check runs every morning against Outlook Sent/Inbox and Salesforce — it starts tracking on any email it finds was actually sent, pulls out anyone who's replied (auto-removing clear "not interested" replies as negative, flagging anything less obvious above for you), and permanently retires anyone who's become a real Salesforce enquiry/opportunity so they're never chased again. Sychem leads aren't covered by that check yet — Outlook can't see Sychem's mailbox from this connection, and Sychem has no CRM to check against — so Sychem still relies on you clicking "Start Follow-Up Tracking" and the outcome buttons yourself. Mailshot content flagged ⚠ is a placeholder template — swap in a real, anonymised recent project before sending; company names should never appear in mailshot copy. 18 Aug fix: tried deep-linking "Open in Outlook — Reply-All" straight into a real Outlook Web thread reply, but that reliably failed (ERR_INVALID_RESPONSE) once actually tested against a live mailbox — the New Outlook client intercepts those links into its own webview and the reply viewmodel doesn't render through it. Reverted to the mailto: link, since that's confirmed to reliably open the real desktop Outlook compose window rather than a browser tab — it's a new email rather than a true header-level reply (mailto: has no way to attach to a real sent item), but the body now quotes a Sent/To/Subject block above your original message, the same layout Outlook's own quoted replies use, so it reads the same way once it lands. A real Reply-All is still possible — it just can't be triggered from this page, only from inside Outlook itself (a static webpage has no way to reach in and fire an Outlook command). That's what the "Follow-Up Reply" Outlook Add-in is for, pending your IT admin deploying it: a "🔎 Open Original Email in Outlook" button appears wherever the real message ID is on file, which jumps straight to that email (this part is confirmed working, unlike the reply deep link) — from there, clicking the add-in's own ribbon button gives a genuine native Reply-All with the suggested text pre-filled. 19 Aug update, link behaviour — resolved: a run of guesses chased this the wrong way — it wasn't a Claude dialog, wasn't Windows Default Apps, wasn't Chrome's installed-apps list, and removing target="_blank" didn't fix it either. Along the way a microsoft-edge: prefix was added to force the link into Edge specifically, which did get it into a real browser tab — but the error that showed there next (OwaUserHasNoMailboxAndNoLicenseAssignedException) was the real giveaway: the browser's Outlook Web session was signed into an account with no licensed mailbox attached, nothing to do with the link itself. Aidan confirmed this directly by diffing a working local copy of this portal against the current one — the link code was byte-for-byte identical in both, proving the link was never the problem. Once signed into the correct aidan@tapflopumps.co.uk account in the browser, the plain link opens the real email immediately. The microsoft-edge: prefix has been removed and target="_blank" restored — back to the original, simplest form, which is correct. Standing rule going forward, this portal and any future one: keep "Open Original Email in Outlook" as a plain https://outlook.office365.com/owa/?ItemID=...&viewmodel=ReadMessageItem link (the same URL Microsoft Graph's own webLink field returns for a message) opened with target="_blank" rel="noopener" — no URI-scheme tricks, no dropping target="_blank". If it ever fails again, check which Microsoft account is signed into the browser before touching this code.

Conversions

Contacts that started as cold outreach on this portal and have since become a genuine, logged Salesforce record — an Enquiry (Lead), Opportunity or Account. Once a contact lands here they're permanently out of the follow-up cascade; this is just a record of the handoff, not something you action from this page.
No conversions yet — this fills in automatically the moment a contact's follow-up status is set to "converted".
